title: Lagrange’s theorem
objectives: Prove Lagrange’s theorem and use it to rule out subgroup sizes.

screens.title: Hunting for three
screens.prose: Can $D_4$ have a subgroup with exactly 3 elements? Pick three elements, $e$ among them, from the first column. Then use the table to test whether their products stay inside.
screens.question: Tap three cells of the first column to pick your three elements.

hints.text: Include e, then try a turn and its undo.
Try $\{e, r, r^3\}$: what is $r \cdot r$?
$r \cdot r = r^2$ escapes; try $\{e, s, r^2\}$: $s \cdot r^2 = r^2s$ escapes too.

feedback.correct: Now test your three with the table: does every product stay among them?
feedback.generic: Pick exactly three cells of the first column.

explain.text: Every choice leaks. With $x \ne e$ in the set, $x^2$ must be $e$ or $x$'s partner, and the products then leave the set. The next screen settles it.

screens.title: None of size 3
screens.prose: The subgroups of $D_4$ from l5 have sizes 1, 2, 4 and 8.
screens.question: Does $D_4$ have a subgroup with exactly 3 elements?

options.text: No. Every subgroup size divides 8, and 3 does not.

options.why: You paired a turn with its undo. $r \cdot r = r^2$ is outside the set.
You chose two elements that undo themselves. $s \cdot r^2 = r^2s$ escapes.

hints.text: List the sizes of all ten subgroups from l5.
Each divides 8; 3 does not, so there is none.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Test the candidate's products.

explain.text: $r \cdot r = r^2$ and $s \cdot r^2 = r^2s$ both escape. Every subgroup of $D_4$ has 1, 2, 4 or 8 elements, all divisors of 8.

screens.title: Lagrange's theorem
screens.prose: **Lagrange's theorem**: if $H$ is a subgroup of a finite group $G$, then $|H|$ divides $|G|$. The number of cosets is the **index** $[G : H] = |G|/|H|$.
screens.question: Order the proof. Leave out the false line.

lines.text: The left cosets of $H$ cover $G$, since $g = ge \in gH$.
Two left cosets are equal or disjoint (l6).
If there are $k$ distinct cosets, then $|G| = k|H|$.
Every subset whose size divides $|G|$ is a coset.
lines.why: You made the cosets from the size. They come from $H$: in $D_4$, $\{e, r\}$ has 2 elements and is no coset.

hints.text: The cosets of H tile the group.
Cover, no overlaps, equal sizes, count.

feedback.correct: That is the proof: the cosets cut G into equal pieces.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Show the cosets cover G before counting them.

byKey.left-out: You left out a step the proof needs.

explain.text: The cosets cover $G$, do not overlap and each has $|H|$ elements. So $|G|$ is $|H|$ times the number of cosets.

screens.title: Reasons for each step
screens.prose: Match each claim in the proof to the reason that makes it true.
screens.question: Drag each reason to its claim.

slots.label: No element lies in two cosets

hints.text: An element $g$ lies in its own coset because $g = ge$.
Cover by g = ge; disjoint by l6; size by the bijection; then count.

feedback.correct: Right. Each step rests on one fact.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Match each claim to the fact it needs.

explain.text: $g = ge$ puts every element in a coset. Equal-or-disjoint stops double counting, and the bijection gives each coset $|H|$ elements.

screens.title: The order of an element
screens.prose: Take $g$ in a finite group $G$. Its powers form the cyclic subgroup $\langle g \rangle$ (l4).
screens.question: Why does $\operatorname{ord}(g)$ divide $|G|$?

options.text: $\langle g \rangle$ is a subgroup with $\operatorname{ord}(g)$ elements, so Lagrange applies.

options.why: You used the consequence as the reason. $g^{|G|} = e$ follows from this fact, not the other way round.
You assumed $|G|$ prime. $D_4$ has 8 elements and the fact still holds.

hints.text: How many elements does $\langle g \rangle$ have?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find a subgroup of size ord(g).

explain.text: $\langle g \rangle$ has exactly $\operatorname{ord}(g)$ elements, so $\operatorname{ord}(g) \mid |G|$. Hence $g^{|G|} = e$ for every $g$. A group of prime order $p$ is cyclic: any $g \ne e$ has order $p$.

screens.title: Possible sizes
screens.prose: A group $G$ has 12 elements. Lagrange limits the sizes its subgroups can have.
screens.question: Select all that apply: which sizes can a subgroup of G have?

options.why: You kept 5. It does not divide 12.
You kept 8. It does not divide 12.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Keep exactly the divisors of 12.

explain.text: Lagrange allows only divisors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. It does not promise each one occurs; the trap shows a gap.

screens.title: Orders modulo 13
screens.prose: $\mathbb{Z}_{13}^{\times}$ has 12 elements, so every order divides 12. The table lists the powers of 2.
screens.question: Fill in the order of each element modulo 13.

hints.text: Multiply until you reach 1; only divisors of 12 can occur.

feedback.correct: Right: 12, 3, 4 and 2, each a divisor of 12.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply by the element until you reach 1.

explain.text: The orders 12, 3, 4, 2 all divide $|\mathbb{Z}_{13}^{\times}| = 12$. The element 2 has order 12, so it generates the whole group.

screens.title: The converse
screens.prose: $A_4$, the even permutations of 4 objects (l9), has 12 elements. Lagrange says its subgroups have sizes among 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12.
screens.question: Must $A_4$ have a subgroup of order 6, since 6 divides 12?

options.text: No. Lagrange's converse is false: $A_4$ has no subgroup of order 6.
Yes: each divisor of the order is the order of some subgroup.
options.why: You reversed Lagrange. It says sizes must divide $|G|$, not that every divisor occurs.

options.text: Yes: a group of order 12 is cyclic, so it has every size.
options.why: You assumed a group of order 12 is cyclic. $A_4$ is not, and neither is $D_6$.

hints.text: Lagrange rules sizes out; it never rules them in.
Is the converse of a theorem automatically true?
A brute-force search of $A_4$ finds subgroups of sizes 1, 2, 3, 4 and 12 only.

feedback.correct: Right. Divisibility is necessary, not sufficient.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Lagrange only forbids sizes.

byKey.yes: You used the converse of Lagrange. $A_4$ is the standard counterexample: no subgroup of order 6.

explain.text: Lagrange gives a necessary condition only. $A_4$ has subgroups of orders 1, 2, 3, 4 and 12 but none of order 6. The homework checks it by brute force.

screens.title: Prime order
screens.question: What can we say about $\langle g \rangle$?

options.text: $\langle g \rangle = G$: its order divides 7 and is not 1, so it is 7.

options.why: You split 7 in two. Only 1 and 7 divide 7.

options.text: It depends on which g we pick.
options.why: You expected some $g$ to fail. Every $g \ne e$ has order 7, so every one generates $G$.

feedback.correct: Right. Every group of prime order is cyclic.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Apply Lagrange to the cyclic subgroup.

explain.text: $|\langle g \rangle|$ divides 7 and exceeds 1, so it is 7 and $\langle g \rangle = G$. The same holds for $|G| = 2$: $G = \{e, g\}$ with $g^2 = e$.

screens.title: Random number generators
screens.prose: A Lehmer generator outputs $x_{k+1} = a x_k \bmod p$. It walks round $\langle a \rangle$ inside $\mathbb{Z}_p^{\times}$, so its period is $\operatorname{ord}(a)$, a divisor of $p - 1$. Modulo 13, $a = 2$ gives the full period 12.

state.caption: The walk x → 3x mod 13 from x = 1

screens.question: What is the period of the generator with $a = 3$ modulo 13?

feedback.correct: Right: it repeats after 3 outputs, a poor generator.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply by 3 modulo 13 until you return to 1.

byKey.full: You assumed every $a$ gives period $p - 1$. Only a generator of $\mathbb{Z}_{13}^{\times}$ does, and 3 has order 3.
byKey.a: You used the modulus. The period is the order of a.

explain.text: $3^3 = 27 \equiv 1 \pmod{13}$, so the outputs cycle $1, 3, 9$: period 3. Lagrange forces the period to divide 12.

screens.title: The minimal standard generator
screens.prose: The minimal standard generator uses the prime $p = 2^{31} - 1 = 2147483647$ and $a = 16807 = 7^5$. We want $\operatorname{ord}(a) = p - 1 = 2147483646 = 2 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 31 \cdot 151 \cdot 331$.
screens.question: Why is it enough to check $a^{(p-1)/q} \ne 1$ for each prime $q$ dividing $p - 1$?

options.text: By Lagrange, $\operatorname{ord}(a)$ divides $p - 1$; a proper divisor divides some $(p - 1)/q$.
Because $a^k \ne 1$ for every $k < p - 1$ follows from $a$ being prime.
options.why: You leaned on $a$. $16807 = 7^5$ is not prime, and primality of $a$ would not decide its order.
You read $a^{p-1} = 1$ as order $p - 1$. Every unit has $a^{p-1} = 1$; the order could be a smaller divisor.

hints.text: If the order were a proper divisor $d$ of $p - 1$, then $d$ divides $(p - 1)/q$ for some prime $q$.
Then $a^{(p-1)/q} = 1$. Ruling that out for each $q$ forces order $p - 1$.

feedback.correct: Right. Seven checks replace two billion.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Use that the order divides p − 1.

explain.text: The order divides $p - 1$. If it were smaller, it would divide $(p - 1)/q$ for some prime $q$, giving $a^{(p-1)/q} = 1$. All seven checks fail to give 1, so $\operatorname{ord}(16807) = p - 1$.

ideas: Lagrange: the cosets of $H$ split $G$ into $[G : H]$ pieces of size $|H|$, so $|H|$ divides $|G|$.
So $\operatorname{ord}(g)$ divides $|G|$, $g^{|G|} = e$, and a group of prime order is cyclic.
The converse fails: $A_4$ has order 12 and no subgroup of order 6.

formula.name: Lagrange
formula.note: For a finite group G and a subgroup H.

summary.trap: A divisor of $|G|$ need not be a subgroup size: $A_4$ has none of size 6.

quiz.question: A group $G$ has exactly 2 elements. Which describes it?

options.why: You set $g^2 = g$. Cancelling $g$ gives $g = e$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. What can g² be?

explain.text: $g^2$ is $e$ or $g$; $g^2 = g$ forces $g = e$. So $g^2 = e$, and $G \cong \mathbb{Z}_2$.
